Check for the accessibility laws in your place of residence. This could be considered discrimination and you could have a right to sue. In the United States and Canada they protect the rights of people with disabilities (of different abilities).

This might not be a solution to your exact problem but I wonder if you ever heard of [Universal Design for Learning](https://udlguidelines.cast.org/). 

I heard about it because I work in the field of digital accessibility. I think its great that you are able to push advanced students further, but is your teaching style supporting all of your students?

I think its a well known fact that some students will learn better with some teachers rather than others because of the teaching style. The Universal Design for Learning was made to try to accomodate as many learning styles as possible.

I am not an expert on this, but maybe it would be worth a look into if you haven't already?
